birthplace: Salt Lake City, Utah, United States
nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the satirist of the Harlem Renaissance
literary_identity: Novelist, playwright and editor; the author of The Blacker the Berry and the great satirist of the Harlem Renaissance.
biography: Born Wallace Henry Thurman in Salt Lake City on 16 August 1902; he studied at the University of Utah and the University of Southern California, moved to Harlem, edited Fire!! in 1926, and published The Blacker the Berry (1929), a play with William Jourdan Rapp, and Infants of the Spring (1932). He died in New York on 22 December 1934.
literary_profile: Wallace Thurman was the great satirist of the Harlem Renaissance: The Blacker the Berry made colour prejudice within the Black community its subject, and Infants of the Spring is the definitive satire of the movement itself, and he edited Fire!!, the most radical of the Harlem magazines.
stylistic_characteristics: The satire of the movement from inside; the Black middle-class interior; the plain, colloquial, unsparing prose; the portrait of the Black woman and colour prejudice; the comedy of the artistic set.
intellectual_concerns: Race, the colour line, and the New Negro; sexuality, the new psychology; the woman question, married disability, and the New Woman; class, the servant problem, and the new democracy.
historical_significance: Wallace Thurman was the great satirist of the Harlem Renaissance: The Blacker the Berry made colour prejudice within the Black community its subject, Infants of the Spring is the definitive satire of the movement itself, and he edited Fire!!, the most radical of the Harlem magazines.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Black satire and the anti-utopia
literary_identity: Journalist and satirist; the author of Black No More, the funniest and most radical Black satire of the period.
biography: Born George Samuel Schuyler in Providence, Rhode Island, on 25 February 1895; he served in the army, worked as a journalist for the Pittsburgh Courier and The Messenger, and published Black No More in 1931, followed by Slaves Today (1931) and Black and Conservative (1966). He died in New York on 31 August 1977.
literary_profile: George Schuyler wrote Black No More, the funniest and most radical Black satire of the period: its premise of a machine that turns Black Americans white made it the definitive satire of American race and one of the founding texts of the Black speculative novel.
stylistic_characteristics: The satirical premise carried to its absurd conclusion; the rapid comic narrative; the caricature of the race leaders and the white liberals; the plain, hard, funny prose; the science-fiction device as social argument.
intellectual_concerns: Race, the colour line, and the New Negro; mass society, the crowd, and the individual talent; money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination; democracy, individualism, and the American experiment.
historical_significance: George Schuyler wrote Black No More, the funniest and most radical Black satire of the period: its premise of a machine that turns Black Americans white made it the definitive satire of American race and one of the founding texts of the Black speculative novel.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Harlem detective story and the Black city
literary_identity: Physician, short-story writer and novelist; the author of The Walls of Jericho and the first Black writer of the Harlem detective story.
biography: Born Rudolph John Chauncey Fisher in Washington, D.C., on 9 May 1897; he studied medicine at Howard and Columbia, worked as a radiologist in New York, and published The Walls of Jericho (1928), The Conjure-Man Dies (1932, the first Black detective novel) and the stories of The City of Refuge. He died in New York on 26 December 1934.
literary_profile: Rudolph Fisher was the first Black writer of the Harlem detective story and one of the finest novelists of the Renaissance: The Walls of Jericho made the Black city its subject, and The Conjure-Man Dies created the Black detective novel and made Harlem the setting of a new kind of American crime fiction.
stylistic_characteristics: The comic novel of Harlem; the detective story with a Black detective; the exact dialect of the city; the medical detail and the autopsy; the plain, witty, rapid prose.
intellectual_concerns: Race, the colour line, and the New Negro; the American city, the machine, and the moneyed metropolis; the Depression, unemployment, and the hunger march; class, the servant problem, and the new democracy.
historical_significance: Rudolph Fisher was the first Black writer of the Harlem detective story: The Walls of Jericho made the Black city its subject, and The Conjure-Man Dies created the Black detective novel and made Harlem the setting of a new kind of American crime fiction.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the philosophy of the New Negro
literary_identity: Philosopher, critic and editor; the editor of The New Negro and the intellectual father of the Harlem Renaissance.
biography: Born Alain Leroy Locke in Philadelphia on 15 September 1885; he was the first Black American Rhodes Scholar, took a doctorate at Harvard, and taught philosophy at Howard University from 1918. The New Negro (1925), The Negro in Art (1940) and his essays on cultural pluralism followed. He died in New York on 9 June 1954.
literary_profile: Alain Locke was the intellectual father of the Harlem Renaissance and the editor of The New Negro, the anthology that defined the movement: his philosophy of cultural pluralism made the case for a Black American art and gave the Renaissance its programme and its name.
stylistic_characteristics: The editorial anthology with its manifesto; the critical essay on the Black arts; the philosophical argument for cultural pluralism; the plain, formal, academic prose; the introduction that frames the whole.
intellectual_concerns: Race, the colour line, and the New Negro; art versus life, and the romance of the artist; education, the schools, and the cultivation of the self; mass society, the crowd, and the individual talent.
historical_significance: Alain Locke was the intellectual father of the Harlem Renaissance and the editor of The New Negro, the anthology that defined the movement: his philosophy of cultural pluralism made the case for a Black American art and gave the Renaissance its programme and its name.

birthplace: Saint Ann's Bay, Jamaica, British West Indies
nationality_or_literary_tradition: Jamaican; the Black nationalism and the public address
literary_identity: Orator, journalist and Black nationalist; the founder of the Universal Negro Improvement Association and the central figure of the Black nationalist movement of the century.
biography: Born Marcus Mosiah Garvey in Saint Ann's Bay, Jamaica, on 17 August 1887; he worked as a printer, travelled in Central America and London, and founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association in Jamaica in 1914, moving it to Harlem in 1916. The Negro World, the Black Star Line and his speeches made him a world figure; he was convicted of mail fraud in 1923 and died in London on 10 June 1940.
literary_profile: Marcus Garvey was the central figure of Black nationalism in the twentieth century: his Universal Negro Improvement Association, his Negro World and his speeches made the case for Black pride and Black self-determination to millions, and his movement is the direct ancestor of the Black nationalism of the century.
stylistic_characteristics: The mass meeting and the oration; the plain, repetitive, incantatory address; the appeal to racial pride; the programme of self-help and return; the direct, emotional, popular rhetoric.
intellectual_concerns: Race, the colour line, and the New Negro; democracy, individualism, and the American experiment; empire, the imperial idea, and its discontents; mass society, the crowd, and the individual talent.
historical_significance: Marcus Garvey was the central figure of Black nationalism in the twentieth century: his Universal Negro Improvement Association, his Negro World and his speeches made the case for Black pride and self-determination to millions, and his movement is the direct ancestor of modern Black nationalism.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the historical detective novel and the mystery of character
literary_identity: Novelist; the pseudonym of Elizabeth Mackintosh, the finest writer of the Golden Age detective novel after Christie and Sayers.
biography: Born Elizabeth Mackintosh at Inverness on 25 July 1896; she trained as a physical education teacher and wrote under the name Gordon Daviot for the stage and Josephine Tey for her crime novels. The Franchise Affair (1948), The Daughter of Time (1951) and Brat Farrar (1949) followed, with the play Richard of Bordeaux (1933). She died in London on 13 February 1952.
literary_profile: Josephine Tey was the finest writer of the Golden Age detective novel after Christie and Sayers: The Daughter of Time reinvented the genre as a historical investigation, The Franchise Affair made the mystery a study of English character, and her work brought a new psychological seriousness to the detective story.
stylistic_characteristics: The detective novel as a study of character; the historical investigation without a corpse; the plain, exact, ironic prose; the English county setting; the surprise solution that turns on human nature.
intellectual_concerns: Class, the servant problem, and the new democracy; the countryside, the vanishing rural world, and the motor road; the absurd, the void; mass society, the crowd, and the individual talent.
historical_significance: Josephine Tey was the finest writer of the Golden Age detective novel after Christie and Sayers: The Daughter of Time reinvented the genre as a historical investigation, and The Franchise Affair made the mystery a study of English character.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: New Zealand-British; the theatre detective and Inspector Alleyn
literary_identity: Novelist and theatre director; one of the four Queens of Crime and the creator of Inspector Roderick Alleyn.
biography: Born Edith Ngaio Marsh in Christchurch, New Zealand, on 23 April 1895; she studied painting, worked in the theatre, and published A Man Lay Dead in 1934, the first of thirty-two Inspector Alleyn novels. She directed Shakespeare in New Zealand and England, and died in Christchurch on 18 February 1982.
literary_profile: Ngaio Marsh was one of the four Queens of Crime and the creator of Inspector Roderick Alleyn: her detective novels brought the theatre into the Golden Age mystery, and her thirty-two novels made her one of the most admired writers of the classical detective story.
stylistic_characteristics: The theatre and the country house as the setting of murder; the aristocratic detective and his assistants; the fair-play plot; the exact social comedy; the plain, elegant, well-made prose.
intellectual_concerns: Class, the servant problem, and the new democracy; the theatre and the actor's world; the countryside, the vanishing rural world, and the motor road; empire, the imperial idea, and its discontents.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Golden Age mystery and Albert Campion
literary_identity: Novelist; one of the four Queens of Crime and the creator of Albert Campion.
biography: Born Margery Louise Allingham in Ealing on 9 May 1904, the daughter of the writer Herbert Allingham; she published The White Cottage Mystery in 1928 and The Crime at Black Dudley, the first Campion novel, in 1929. Tiger in the Smoke (1952), The Tiger in the Smoke's predecessor The Fashion in Shrouds (1938) and The Beckoning Lady (1955) followed. She died at Colchester on 30 June 1966.

stylistic_characteristics: The comic detective and the grotesque villain; the London fog and the country house; the Dickensian minor character; the thriller plot inside the mystery; the plain, lively, inventive prose.
